sections.h: Galatians 1-3: no other good news, and Abraham's children by faith
sections.b: The first three chapters open with a rebuke and a curse on any other good news (1:6-10), tell Paul's story from his call through the Jerusalem meeting and the clash with Cephas at Antioch (1:11-2:14), and state the good news: justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, crucified with Christ (2:15-21). They then argue from the Galatians' experience of the Spirit and from Abraham that those who are from faith are Abraham's sons, that the law is temporary, and that in Christ there is no Jew and no Greek, no slave and no free person, no male and female (3:1-29).

common: Galatians is by Paul, and its main argument is that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the law of Moses to belong to God's people.
uncommon: Mark Nanos reads the 'agitators' as Jewish teachers outside the Christian groups, and J. Louis Martyn reads the whole letter as a report of God's apocalyptic invasion of the world.

sections.b: Paul writes to 'the churches of Galatia' (1:2). The old region of Galatia lay around Ancyra; the Roman province also took in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, where Acts 13-14 records Paul and Barnabas planting churches. The North and South Galatian views disagree about which Paul means, and the choice affects the date of the letter and its relation to Acts 15.
sections.refs: Galatians 1:2; Galatians 3:1; Acts 13:14; Acts 14:6; Acts 16:6; Acts 18:23

sections.b: Paul uses the phrase in 2:16 (three times), 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10. In 2:16 it is the thing by which no flesh will be justified; in 3:2 and 3:5 the Galatians are asked whether they received the Spirit by it; in 3:10 'all who are from works of the law are under a curse'. The New Perspective takes it as the Jewish practices that marked off Israel; the traditional Protestant reading as all that the law requires; Catholic teaching adds that no works of human strength or of the law justify without grace.

common: Almost all scholars agree that Paul sets 'works of the law' against faith in Christ.
uncommon: The Dead Sea text 4QMMT ('Some of the Works of the Torah') has the Hebrew phrase in its title, and some scholars compare it with Paul's phrase.

sections.b: Paul calls them 'some people who are upsetting you' (1:7) and 'false brothers' (2:4), and he says that Cephas, by withdrawing, 'compels the Gentiles to live in the Jewish way' (2:14). Mirror-reading the letter shows teachers who pressed Gentile believers to be circumcised, probably appealing to Genesis 17.

sections.b: At Antioch Cephas ate with the Gentile believers until some people came from James, then drew back, and the other Jews and Barnabas followed. Paul opposed Cephas to his face, in front of the whole church (2:11-14). Whether the incident came before or after the Council of Acts 15 is disputed.

Paul names Barnabas as the companion who went with him to Jerusalem (2:1) and who shook hands with the pillars on the Gentile mission (2:9). At Antioch he was 'carried away' by the Jewish believers' withdrawal (2:13), which Paul seems to have felt as a loss, since Barnabas had been his partner.

sections.h: Faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ in Galatians
sections.b: The phrase occurs in 2:16 (twice), 2:20 and 3:22, with a related 'faith in Christ Jesus' in 3:26. The Plain English Translation follows 'faith in Jesus Christ' (as at Romans 3:22) and gives the other reading in a variant entry at 2:16 and 3:22. In 3:22 the objective reading is hardest, since the verse already speaks of 'those who believe'; in 2:16 the clause 'we also believed in Christ Jesus' supports it.

'Flesh' appears in four senses in these chapters: ordinary human beings ('flesh and blood', 1:16); the body and its life ('the life I now live in the flesh', 2:20); human weakness ('no flesh will be justified', 2:16); and the sphere of human effort set against the Spirit ('finish in the flesh', 3:3). The word's darker sense is developed in 5:13-26.

The word 'freedom' first appears in 2:4: the false brothers slipped in to scout out 'our freedom, which we hold in Christ Jesus', so that they will make us slaves. Paul will not give way, 'so that the truth of the good news would continue with you'. The theme returns at 3:28 ('no slave and no free person') and is developed in 4:21-5:13.

Galatians 2:11-16 and 3:6-14 are the main places where the New Perspective differs from the older Protestant reading. Dunn reads 'works of the law' as boundary markers and the Antioch table as the setting for the doctrine of justification; Wright reads 3:10-14 as the story of Israel's curse and exile ended in Christ. Critics (Moo, Schreiner) answer that 3:10 speaks of the whole law and of human inability.

At Antioch Cephas ate with the Gentile believers and then drew back, 'because he was afraid of those from the circumcision' (2:12). Paul called it acting a part, and said that it forced Gentiles to live in the Jewish way (2:13-14). The story is the most important case of table fellowship across the Jew-Gentile line in the New Testament.

Paul took Titus, a Greek, with him to Jerusalem, and Titus was not made to get circumcised (2:1-3). It is Paul's test case: a Gentile believer, a colleague of the apostle, uncircumcised in front of the Jerusalem leaders.

The Jerusalem leaders asked only one thing, that Paul and Barnabas remember the poor, and Paul says he was eager to do that. His later collections from his Gentile churches (1 Corinthians 16:1-4, which mentions 'the churches of Galatia'; 2 Corinthians 8-9; Romans 15:25-31) keep the promise.

In Galatians 2:16 Paul says that a person 'is not justified by works of the law, except through faith in Jesus Christ'. The verse makes the Antioch dispute a question of justification: who is in the right with God, and who belongs to God's family. Abraham is the example (3:6), and Habakkuk 2:4 the text (3:11). The churches' answers are set out at 2:16 and in the book introduction; they differ on what 'justified' means, on how faith and works relate, and on 'works of the law'.

common: Almost all traditions agree that Galatians teaches that no one is justified by the law of Moses apart from Christ.
uncommon: The New Perspective reads justification as the declaration of who belongs to God's family, here in a dispute about Jews and Gentiles at one table.

sections.b: Faith is the central idea of chapters 2-3: 'we believed in Christ Jesus' (2:16), 'the hearing of faith' (3:2, 5), Abraham who 'believed God' (3:6), 'those who are from faith' (3:7, 9), Habakkuk's 'The righteous will live by faith' (3:11), and 'this faith came' (3:23, 25). Whether Paul sometimes means Christ's faithfulness (pistis Christou) is debated.

Paul says that the law cannot justify (2:16), that he died to the law through the law (2:19), that it brings a curse on those who rely on it (3:10), that it was added 430 years after the promise on account of transgressions, through angels and a mediator (3:17-19), and that it was an attendant until Christ (3:24-25). He also says it is not against the promises of God (3:21). Churches differ on its uses, on whether Jewish believers should keep it, and on what the ending of the attendant means.

Titus was not circumcised (2:3), the Jerusalem leaders did not require it of Gentiles (2:6-9), and Paul resisted the 'false brothers' who did (2:4-5). The agitators in Galatia asked it of the Gentile believers (5:2-3; 6:12-13), probably on the basis of Genesis 17:9-14. Paul does not mention Genesis 17 in the letter; he goes back to Genesis 12 and 15.

Paul presents Abraham as the believer to whom the good news was told ahead of time: he 'believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness' (3:6; Genesis 15:6), and 'All the nations will be blessed in you' (3:8; Genesis 12:3). Those who are from faith are his sons (3:7), the law came 430 years after the promise to him (3:17), and those who belong to Christ are his offspring and heirs (3:29).

Paul uses an everyday example: once a human covenant (or will) is ratified, no one cancels it or adds to it (3:15). The covenant with Abraham was confirmed by God 430 years before the law, which cannot cancel it (3:17). Whether he is thinking of one covenant or two is debated; in the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (4:21-31) he speaks of two.

sections.h: Paul's call and early career in Galatians 1-2
sections.b: Paul tells his own story in 1:11-2:14: a zealous persecutor, called by God's grace and given a revelation of the Son; Arabia and Damascus; fifteen days with Cephas and James in Jerusalem three years later; Syria and Cilicia; and a second visit fourteen years later with Barnabas and Titus. He insists that he did not receive the good news from any human being.

Paul went up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas and stayed fifteen days (1:18). Cephas is named a pillar and entrusted with the good news for the circumcised (2:7-9). At Antioch Paul opposed him to his face because he stood under condemnation (2:11-14). Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers differ on what the episode shows about Peter's place in the church.

sections.h: James the Lord's brother in Galatians
sections.b: Paul calls James 'the brother of the Lord' (1:19), names him first among the pillars (2:9), and says that the people who came to Antioch were 'from James' (2:12). The churches differ on whether he was a younger brother, a stepbrother or a cousin of Jesus; see the card at 1:19.

Paul's first question to the Galatians is whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by the hearing of faith (3:2), and his second whether God supplies the Spirit and works powerful works among them by one or the other (3:5). He then says that the blessing of Abraham reaches the Gentiles 'so that we would receive the promise of the Spirit through faith' (3:14).

Whether the meeting Paul describes in 2:1-10 is the same as the meeting of Acts 15 is one of the main questions of New Testament history. If it is, Galatians was written afterward, and Paul's silence about the apostolic decree needs an explanation. If it is the famine visit of Acts 11:30, Galatians was written before the Council. See the chapter page.

Paul reads the singular 'offspring' of the promises to Abraham as meaning Christ: 'The text does not say, "and to offsprings," as in the case of many, but as in the case of one, "and to your offspring." That one is Christ.' In 3:29 those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, so the one and the many are united.

sections.h: The curse of the law in Galatians 3:10-14
sections.b: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 and 21:23 to say that those who are from works of the law are under a curse and that Christ became a curse for us, so that Abraham's blessing might reach the Gentiles (3:10-14). The reading of the curse as every person's failure, as Israel's exile, or as the effect of misusing the law is debated.

Paul speaks of being 'crucified together with Christ' (2:20), says the cross was put before the Galatians' eyes as on a public notice (3:1), and says that Christ became a curse in hanging on a tree (3:13).

Paul opens by saying he is an apostle 'not from people, and not through any human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father' (1:1), and spends 1:11-2:10 on the source of his message and his standing with the Jerusalem apostles.

Paul says that 'even an angel from heaven' who preaches a different good news is accursed (1:8), and that the law was 'arranged through angels, by the hand of a mediator' (3:19), a tradition shared with Deuteronomy 33:2 (Greek), Acts 7:53 and Hebrews 2:2.
Paul says that all who believe are 'sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus' (3:26) and heirs by the promise (3:29). Adoption into God's family is developed in 4:5-7.

'Every one of you who was baptized into Christ has put Christ on' (3:27). Paul uses baptism as the point at which the divisions of 3:28 are overcome. Churches differ on what baptism does; see the card at 3:27.

Paul's third pair, 'male and female', uses the wording of Genesis 1:27 and goes beyond the first two. Churches agree that the verse states the equal standing of men and women in Christ; they differ on whether it bears on the offices of the church. See the card at 3:28.

sections.h: 'No Jew and no Greek' in Galatians 3:28
sections.b: Paul says that in Christ Jesus 'there is no Jew and no Greek', and that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs. Readers differ on whether this ends Jewish identity in the church, ends only Jewish privilege, or says that Jew and Gentile are one family without becoming alike. See the card at 3:28.

sections.h: 'No slave and no free person' in Galatians 3:28
sections.b: Paul puts slave and free beside Jew and Greek and male and female in a single formula. He does not call in this letter for the end of slavery, but the verse was cited by abolitionists. See the note at 3:28 and Philemon.

sections.h: The curse and the cross in Galatians 1:4; 2:20; 3:13
sections.b: Galatians has three short statements on the meaning of Christ's death: he 'gave himself for our sins' to take us out of the present evil age (1:4); he 'loved me and gave himself up for me' (2:20); and he 'bought us free from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us' (3:13). The churches read them as sacrifice, satisfaction, penal substitution, victory over death, or Israel's representative taking the exile. See the card at 3:10-14.

Papyrus 46 (about AD 200) has all of Galatians; Papyrus 51 has parts of chapter 1. The notable variants in chapters 1-3 are at 1:6, 1:15, 1:18 (Cephas or Peter), 2:5 (a Western omission of 'not'), 2:9 (the order of the pillars), 2:12, 2:20 ('faith in the Son of God' or 'in God and Christ'), 3:1, 3:14 and 3:17.
